source: Stocker (2026) Towards Persistent Case-Based Memory for Autonomous Data Science: a CBR-augmented R&D-Agent with a small language model
finding: A persistent case base with a reuse check was tested against the same agent with retrieval switched off. Token cost was counted. Results split by task: better on one, slightly worse on the other.
numbers: Gemma 4 31B, 4 seeds x 8 improvement loops, 2 Kaggle tasks. Spaceship Titanic accuracy 0.8147 vs 0.8098 (CBR vs off, d=-1.41, p=0.11, lower variance). NOMAD RMSLE 0.0632 vs 0.0608 (CBR worse, d=-0.75, p=0.20). Prompt tokens on Spaceship Titanic 929k vs 625k (+49%, p=0.029). Seed library 60 cases, grew to 67-68. 108 retrieval events, all above both reuse thresholds (embedding 0.82, code fingerprint 0.10); no event was rejected. Mean embedding similarity 0.882, mean code fingerprint similarity 0.305.
quote: causing the agent to generate hypotheses anchored to that level rather than exploring more aggressively
limits: n=4 per cell, no significant score difference, authors call it exploratory. No ablation of what was retrieved. Cases come from the same two tasks. The anchoring explanation for NOMAD is marked post hoc by the author.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 4: a counted-token comparison exists but shows no clear win, and a reuse check that never fires has no power to prevent harm. Gap 5: even high-similarity retrieval (0.88) may reduce exploration.

source: Dong and Shang (2026) Online Boundary-Aware Memory for Case-Based Reasoning Agents (ICML 2026)
finding: Plain retrieve-similar-cases memory gives modest gains over zero-shot on four classification-style CBR tasks. Storing every case slightly lowers accuracy compared with storing selectively. Retrieving too few or too many cases lowers accuracy.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4, accuracy (CaseHOLD / DDXPlus / Phishing / Reviews): zero-shot 0.788/0.753/0.805/0.593; fixed few-shot 0.796/0.775/0.847/0.625; Self-StreamICL (store and retrieve similar cases) 0.807/0.862/0.894/0.650; AWM 0.805/0.807/0.882/0.635; Mem0 0.812/0.851/0.891/0.648; OBAM 0.825/0.919/0.926/0.663. Mistral Large 3 shows the same order. 5 runs, 95% intervals 0.6-0.8 points wide. Sensitivity: retrieving 1 region case instead of 5 loses 7-8 points; saturates at 5 (no gain at 7); retrieving 4 boundary entries instead of 2 slightly worse; interior storage rate 0.1 loses 3-7 points.
quote: storing all interior cases increases memory size linearly while slightly degrading accuracy
limits: Authors' own method. The store-all-interior ablation is a figure; its exact number was not read. Classification tasks with a ground-truth label at retain time, so no judge error. Gain of plain case memory over zero-shot is small on the legal task (+1.9 points).
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a k curve with saturation at about 5 and a drop when conflicting cases are added. Gap 5: near a decision boundary similar cases carry conflicting outcomes, a direct harm mechanism. Gap 10 hint: benefit is largest where zero-shot is weak (DDXPlus +10.9) and small where it is strong.

source: Hu, Long and Wang (2026) When Continual Learning Moves to Memory: A Study of Experience Reuse in LLM Agents
finding: Raw trajectory memory helps inside one task but can hurt when reused on a different task. The harm falls mainly on instances the agent could not already solve. A distilled insight memory is safer across tasks but weaker inside the same task.
numbers: ALFWorld pick_and_place (A, 95% no-memory) to pick_clean_place (B, 54%): Raw scratch 80.5 vs after transfer 71.0 (forward transfer -9.5); Insight 65.5 vs 72.0 (+6.5). On B, instances the no-memory agent failed (n=46): Raw -26.1 points, Insight +3.3. Instances it already solved: Raw +4.6, Insight +9.3. BabyAI A to B: Raw 53.5 vs 46.0 (-7.5; hard instances -12.7); Insight 46.0 vs 55.0 (+9.0; hard +9.8). 100 test instances per phase, 2 runs, retrieval top-1, successes and failures both stored.
quote: raw trajectories can carry over procedures that look relevant but miss the additional structure the harder task requires
limits: Small test sets, 2 runs, one backbone family, top-1 only. Cross-task retrieval is the low-similarity end by design. The reverse direction (hard to easy) shows little gap.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 5: measured harm from a retrieved case from a different task, concentrated where the agent needs help most. Gap 7: distilled beats raw only across tasks; within-task raw is better (80.5 vs 65.5 on ALFWorld B). This narrows the ReasoningBank claim.

source: Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir and Narayanan (2024) AI Agents That Matter
finding: Complex agents with reflection or debugging were compared with plain retry baselines at measured dollar cost. Simple baselines matched them at much lower cost.
numbers: HumanEval, 164 problems, 5 runs each. No significant accuracy difference between a retry-with-rising-temperature baseline (up to 5 tries, temperature 0 to 0.5, retry on failing example tests) and the best agent. Reflexion and LDB cost over 50% more than that baseline; LATS cost over 50 times more. An escalation strategy (cheap model first, stronger model on failure) beat LDB with GPT-3.5 in accuracy at under half the cost.
quote: Accuracy alone cannot identify progress because it can be improved by scientifically meaningless methods such as retrying
limits: Code task with example tests available. The authors say reflection may help on harder tasks such as SWE-bench; not tested. Not about case libraries.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 6: the standard for any case-library or revise-step claim should be accuracy at equal dollar cost against retry. Almost no case-memory paper reports it.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han and Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Survey of self-correction work. Success needs a reliable outside check. Feedback from a prompted copy of the same model does not show reliable gains outside a few well-suited tasks.
numbers: Three main findings stated by the authors: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except in tasks exceptionally suited for it; (2) self-correction works well on tasks that can use reliable external feedback; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction. Many prior comparisons were judged unfair because they compared against weak first answers.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Review, not a new experiment. Judgement of which studies were fair is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a CHEF-style explain-the-failure step in Revise is only expected to help if its failure signal comes from a check outside the model. This matches K20.

source: Mallen, Asai, Zhong, Das, Khashabi and Hajishirzi (2023) When Not to Trust Language Models: Effectiveness of Parametric and Non-Parametric Memories
finding: Retrieval helps on rare facts and is useless or harmful on popular facts the model already knows. Retrieving only when the question is below a popularity threshold beat always retrieving.
numbers: PopQA, GPT-3 davinci-003 with Contriever retrieval: for 10% of questions the model was right alone but wrong with retrieved text (retriever recall@1 on those 0.14); 24% right both ways. Adaptive retrieval gave 46.5% accuracy, 5.3 points above the best non-adaptive method. Models under 10B parameters gain much less from adaptive retrieval because they must retrieve for almost all questions; GPT-3 retrieves for about 40% with BM25.
quote: For 10% of questions, retrieval is harmful due to low-quality retrieved text
limits: Factual QA, not agent tasks. The skip rule uses entity popularity as a proxy for what the model knows, with a threshold tuned per relationship type.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the closest measured answer to when to skip retrieval. A harm rate of about 10% of items was seen for a mixed-quality retriever. The agent analogue is the no-memory pass rate on that problem type, used as the skip trigger.

source: Shi, Chen, Misra, Scales, Dohan, Chi, Scharli and Zhou (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to a math problem sharply cuts accuracy. Distractors that share topic or entity roles with the problem hurt most. Examples that show how to ignore distractors, or a plain instruction to ignore, reduce the damage.
numbers: GSM-IC, 4,000-item sample covering 100 base problems. code-davinci-002 chain-of-thought micro accuracy: in-topic distractor 63.1 vs off-topic 80.7; role-overlap yes 68.3 vs no 76.6. Fewer than 30% of base problems stayed solved across all distractor variants. Exemplars that contain distractors lifted in-topic micro accuracy from 63.1 to 70.2 for chain-of-thought.
limits: Arithmetic with a single synthetic distractor, 2023 models. Not retrieval of cases, but the same mechanism: text that looks relevant and is not.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 5: high topical or role overlap with the problem is when an irrelevant case is most dangerous, so similarity ranking alone picks the worst distractors. A cheap mitigation is to show the model what to ignore.

source: Yoran, Wolfson, Ram and Berant (2024) Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context (ICLR 2024)
finding: Retrieval lowers accuracy on implicit reasoning questions and with random passages. A small entailment filter on the retrieved text prevents the loss but also drops helpful passages. Fine-tuning on mixed relevant and irrelevant contexts removes most of the trade-off.
numbers: Five QA sets. In-context retrieval raised accuracy on single-hop and explicit sets but lowered it on the implicit-reasoning sets StrategyQA and Fermi. Random retrieved passages cut accuracy by more than 10 points on average for in-context use; an NLI filter (BART-large-MNLI, 407M parameters) mitigated this. 1,000 training examples were enough to train the robust model.
quote: retrieval augmentation can sometimes have a negative effect on performance
limits: QA with web or Wikipedia passages, not solved-problem cases. The NLI filter needs a question-answer pair, so it works after a draft answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 8: a cheap structural check at the reuse step exists in a neighbouring field and works, at a cost in recall. Reasoning-heavy items are where retrieved text most often hurts.

source: Olausson, Inala, Wang, Gao and Solar-Lezama (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-repair (explain the failure, then repair) was compared with plain i.i.d. resampling at equal cost. Gains are small, uneven and sometimes absent. The explanation step is the bottleneck: better explanations from a stronger model or a human raise repair success.
numbers: HumanEval and APPS with Code Llama 13B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; cost counted as tokens (pass@t) as well as samples. APPS: GPT-3.5 marginal gains only at the largest sample budgets; GPT-4 up to 8% above baseline; relative gain up to 34% for GPT-3.5 on competition-level problems. HumanEval: gains marginal or absent at small budgets. Repair success with GPT-4's own explanation 33.30% vs 52.60% with human explanations (1.58x); by difficulty 42.64 vs 62.21 (introductory), 19.33 vs 45.67 (interview), 3.67 vs 14.67 (competition). 16 participants, 40 failing programs, 2 human explanations each.
limits: Code with unit tests as the failure signal. Single-trajectory repair trees, not a long-lived library. The human study is small.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the best equal-token test of an explain-the-failure revise step. With the model's own explanation it does not beat resampling by much. A CHEF-style Revise should be run with an outside signal or a stronger explainer, and compared at equal tokens.

source: Bertsch, Ivgi, Alon, Berant, Gormley and Neubig (2025) In-Context Learning with Long-Context Models: An In-Depth Exploration
finding: As the number of demonstrations grows, the advantage of retrieving similar examples over random ones shrinks to a few points. Performance keeps rising with more demonstrations on tasks with large label spaces.
numbers: Banking-77 (retrieval's best case): BM25 retrieval advantage over random selection falls from 51.5 points at 1 demonstration to 4.9 points at 1,500. The gap between BM25 and BERTScore retrieval vanishes at large k. On summarization (SAMSum) retrieval sometimes underperformed random choice at 250-shot.
limits: Classification tasks with labelled demonstrations and long-context models; not agent trajectories. The gain from more demonstrations is task dependent.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: one curve of how much similarity-based case choice matters as k grows. Choice matters at small k and little at large k, so for a token-limited agent at k near 4 the retrieval key matters.

source: Stechly, Marquez and Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems
finding: A GPT-4 judge of its own graph-colouring answers almost never accepts a solution and is rarely right when it does. Self-critique loops lowered accuracy. With a sound external checker the gain came from extra tries, not from the feedback content.
numbers: Graph colouring, 100 instances. No-feedback baseline 16%. Same-model critique loop: 1 of 100 correct. Verification test: of 500 candidate colourings (118 correct), GPT-4 called 30 correct and was right 5 times (precision about 17%, recall about 4%); of 100 optimal colourings it accepted 2. With a sound verifier, accuracy near 40% for pass/fail, first-error and full-error feedback alike; 15 independent samples at temperature 1 with the same verifier also reached about 40%.
quote: blindfolded guessing does just as well as careful, crafted feedback
limits: One NP-complete task, GPT-4 only. It is a result about an LLM judge for reasoning answers, which is the retain-rule judge of gap 3.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a measured LLM-judge precision of about 17 percent on a reasoning task, far too low for selective adding to beat adding nothing. Also gap 6: the informativeness of the failure message did not matter; resampling with the same number of tries matched it.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen and Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings of ACL 2024)
finding: Mistake finding is the weak step. When told the true mistake location, models repair and net accuracy rises. Random locations help much less and cost more on traces that were already right.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 2,186 chain-of-thought traces (generated by PaLM 2 Unicorn, 5 tasks). GPT-4 best at finding the first wrong step but only 52.87 overall accuracy with step-level prompting. Backtracking at the true mistake location: traces with a correct answer lost 0 to 11.43 points (word sorting -11.11) and traces with a wrong answer gained 18.04 to 43.92 (word sorting +23.53). With a random location, correct-answer traces lost 6.67 to 15.91 and wrong-answer traces gained 5.16 to 21.57.
limits: Reasoning traces with step labels; oracle location is not available to an agent. Per-task row mapping of the garbled table was not fully verified; ranges are across the five tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 6: a worked cost of false positives. A wrongly flagged item loses 7-11 points while a true positive gains 18-44, so a judge must clear a precision break-even. The paper gives the ingredients but does not compute it.

source: Agarwal, Singh, Zhang et al. (2024) Many-Shot In-Context Learning (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: On MATH, ordinary in-context learning with ground-truth solutions rises with more examples, peaks, then declines. Using problems only (no solutions) matches or beats showing human solutions. This points to priming by problem distribution and format rather than reuse of the solution.
numbers: MATH500: ICL with ground-truth solutions peaks at about 125 examples then falls; Reinforced ICL (model-generated correct rationales) plateaus at about 25 examples, about 5% above ICL, with no big drop at very large counts; Unsupervised ICL (problems only) matches or beats ground-truth ICL. Mean of 5 seeds. Transfer to GSM8K from MATH prompts also reported.
quote: many-shot ICL achieves comparable or superior performance when using only problems compared to using problems with solutions
limits: One model family. Maths pretraining may already contain the skill, so solutions look redundant. Not a case-retrieval study.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 and 2: supports the worry that part of the case-memory gain is priming. A format-matched irrelevant-case control is still missing for agents, but this shows such a control would be informative. The decline after about 125 examples is one number for the LLM utility problem.

source: Xiong, Lin, Xie et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following behavior (re-read for harm and judge error)
finding: Re-read of the full paper for harm and judge quality. A variant with error-free outputs for the same retrieved cases gives a gap measure of what stored mistakes cost. Harm is shown through that gap, not counted per retrieved case.
numbers: Output similarity tracks input similarity to a near-perfect Pearson correlation when memory is large (the agent copies the nearest case). Every addition rule trails the error-free variant, and add-all and coarse selective addition widen the gap over the run. With a strict evaluator plus history-based deletion, AgentDriver exceeded its error-free memory. Even entries stored under a strict evaluator that had error above 0.5 propagated errors more easily and were removed by history-based deletion.
limits: Four agent types, one synthetic. No count of how many retrievals hurt. The strict evaluator uses ground truth or human labels.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 4: the nearest published stand-in for a harm rate is the utility score of a record (output quality after it is retrieved), used to delete records. A per-case harm count could be built from the same log.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky and Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet (re-read for uncurated history and harm cases)
finding: Appending the full uncurated history can lower accuracy below the no-memory baseline; curated memory does not. Memory can also hurt on knowledge tasks for a mid-strength model.
numbers: AIME 2024: GPT-4o baseline 20.0, full-history append 6.7, DC-RS 40.0; Claude 3.5 Sonnet baseline 23.3, full-history 26.7, DC-Cu 50.0. GPT-4o MMLU-Pro Engineering: baseline 53.2, DC-Cu 44.0 (-9.2), DC-RS 51.2. Claude MMLU-Pro Engineering 61.2 baseline, 57.2 with the empty-memory scaffold (DC-), 67.6 with DC-RS. GPQA Diamond GPT-4o 57.1 baseline and 57.1 under DC-RS.
quote: retrieval can, in some cases, introduce confusion, especially if suboptimal examples are recalled
limits: Small sets (AIME has 30 questions per year). Token counts per condition were not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4, 8 and 10: shows a per-task harm (-9.2) and that uncurated history is the worst arm, on tasks with no environment check.
